newsitem.title: UK: POLL - UK Labour widens lead on economy - Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: POLL - UK Labour widens lead on economy - Reuters poll.

text.p: British voters trust the opposition Labour party more than the ruling Conservatives to manage the economy and the margin has widened, particularly among a crucial sector of voters, a poll by NOP for Reuters showed on Wednesday.

The survey of 1,093 adults, conducted by polling organisation NOP on Tuesday, showed 36 percent trust Labour to manage the economy against 27 percent who have faith in Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives.
The margin in favour of the opposition widened to nine points from five in the last Reuters-NOP poll on April 7.

Conducted ahead of Britain's parliamentary election on Thursday, the poll gave the Labour party a 22-point lead over the Conservatives in terms of total share of the vote. NOP's adjusted figures were 50 percent for Labour, 28 percent for the Conservatives, 14 percent for the Liberal Democrats and eight percent for other parties.

Economists in the City of London say that although the economy is in a fairly healthy state, with steady growth, falling unemployment and low inflation, voters have not given the government the credit.
"While the economy is doing very well, memories of past failings remain vivid," economists Paul Mortimer-Lee and Ken Wattret of Paribas wrote in a report on the market impact of Thursday's election.
The most serious failing was sterling's humiliating exit from the European Union's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) in 1992.
"The resulting recession, decline in house prices and surge in unemployment still haunt the electorate's memory," the Paribas economists said.
"Economic success has come despite Mr Major, not because of him. Little wonder that the electorate's opinion of the Conservatives' economic credentials has fallen in the last five years."
Under the leadership of Tony Blair, Labour has worked hard to ditch its image as a party of high taxes and high public spending.
It has promised not to raise income tax rates, to be firm in fighting inflation and maintain iron control over state finances.
The Reuters/NOP poll showed the Conservatives ahead on the issue of economic competence only among voters in professional and management occupations.

But Labour substantially widened its lead on the economy among so-called "C2" skilled manual workers -- whose support was crucial to the success of former Conservative Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher -- to 20 points in the latest survey from 12 points on April 7.
The Labour party enjoyed an eight-point lead when voters were asked under which party they expect to be better off.
Thirty-six percent of respondents thought they would be better off under Labour compared with 28 percent who expect to be more prosperous under the Conservatives.
Responses once again divided along class lines, with Labour enjoying a 23-point lead among C2 voters while the Conservatives were well ahead only among professionals and managers.
"There seems to have been quite a major turnround since the last election in voters' perceptions of the respective abilities of each party in terms of economic management," Wattret of Paribas said.

"It may reflect a perception among the electorate, contrary to the Conservative election campaign, not that Britain is booming but that certain parts of the economy are performing very well but that is not reflected across the board."
